the nutritional and inflammatory status of African Americans and Caucasians with ESRD and the impact of these factors on survival.

understanding how the nutritional and inflammatory axis of racial survival disparities in dialysis is manifested at the cellular and molecular levels.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the combination of protein-energy wasting, inflammation, oxidative stress and other factors such as atherosclerosis are the most important factors that contribute to the increased risk for cardiovascular disease, hospitalizations and mortality in dialysis patient populations.
the association of PEW and inflammatory markers in dialysis patients is not only related to mortality but it is also related to the development of cardiovascular disease (CVD).
the combination of inflammation, malnutrition, oxidative stress and atherosclerosis is a major contributor to the excess mortality observed in patients with end stage renal disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nutritional and inflammatory axes in dialysis are interdependent, and both contribute to the increased mortality in this population.

the combination of inflammation and protein energy wasting (PE) in patients on dialysis is a powerful predictor of mortality and that this combination is associated with increased oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular disease.
PEW and inflammation are associated with increased mortality in patients undergoing dialysis and that the combination of both conditions may be associated with an even higher mortality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is an inflammatory axis to the survival disparities that we see in African Americans.
the inflammatory axis is a major contributor to the racial disparity in survival in dialysis.
the association between protein intake and mortality is stronger for African Americans than for Caucasians.
